item.title: No charges yet against father and son as Police investigate alleged Sigatoka assault
item.description: No charges have yet been laid against the father and son who remain in Police custody following the alleged assault of a 38-year-old man and his two 16-year-old sons in Mateqe, Sigatoka on Sunday. The 38-year-old, Vimal Nand, later died at the Nadi Hospital.
item.content:encoded:
No charges have yet been laid against the father and son who remain in Police custody following the alleged assault of a 38-year-old man and his two 16-year-old sons in Mateqe, Sigatoka on Sunday.

The 38-year-old, Vimal Nand, later died at the Nadi Hospital.

Police have confirmed to fijivillage News that investigations are still ongoing.

It is alleged that Nand and his sons were assaulted by the two suspects following a confrontation over an incident involving one of Nand’s farm animals.

Police earlier said that a postmortem examination will be conducted to determine the cause of death.

Meanwhile, a Sigatoka resident has alleged that the suspects were drunk at the time and had brutally assaulted Nand and his two sons.

item.title: Raised with Love, now giving love: Youth pastor Nancy Cakacaka shares her story on fijivillage HerStory at 7pm tomorrow
item.description: Nancy Cakacaka is a senior pastor’s wife, a youth pastor, a mentor and a woman dedicated to shaping the next generation. Lovingly known as Aunty Nancy by many young people in her community, she has devoted much of her life to guiding youths, strengthening their Christian faith and encouraging them to make positive choices.
item.content:encoded:
Nancy Cakacaka is a senior pastor’s wife, a youth pastor, a mentor and a woman dedicated to shaping the next generation.

Lovingly known as Aunty Nancy by many young people in her community, she has devoted much of her life to guiding youths, strengthening their Christian faith and encouraging them to make positive choices.

On this week’s fijivillage HerStory with Temalesi Vono, Nancy opens up about her own journey, from growing up in Bua with her grandparents after her parents separated, to the values of love, faith and discipline that shaped her upbringing.

She also shares her experiences working with young people, the challenges families and youths face today, and her message to young people to listen to their parents, stay grounded in their faith and know that they are loved.

Join us at 7pm tomorrow for fijivillage HerStory with Temalesi Vono, as we hear Aunty Nancy's story.

item.title: Four arrested in Lautoka drug raids
item.description: Four people have been arrested following two separate drug raids conducted by the Joint Task Force in Lautoka. Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe says the raids were yesterday in Tavakubu and Vio Road.
item.content:encoded:
Four people have been arrested following two separate drug raids conducted by the Joint Task Force in Lautoka.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe says the raids were yesterday in Tavakubu and Vio Road.

In the first raid in Tavakubu, an 18-year-old student and a 24-year-old man were allegedly found with white substances believed to be methamphetamine.

Both suspects were taken into custody while the seized substances were sent for analysis.

In the second raid at Vio Road, a 38-year-old man and a 37-year-old woman were arrested following the discovery of several plastics containing white substances believed to be illicit drugs.

Police also seized local and foreign currency believed to be proceeds of crime.

The substances seized during the raid have been sent for analysis.

Vusonilawe says successful raids conducted by the Joint Task Force and routine operations teams are a result of intelligence sharing and tips received from members of the public .

The Fiji Police Force is urging members of the public to report drug-related activities through the 1681 toll-free number.

item.title: Ratu Sukuna Rd residents call for action over speeding and reckless driving
item.description: Residents living along Ratu Sukuna Road in Suva are raising concerns about speeding and reckless driving, particularly during weekends when the seawall area becomes a popular recreational area. Ratu Sukuna Road resident Marita Manley, who regularly walks and runs along the seawall with her dog, says the problem is particularly noticeable on Saturday and Sunday afternoons and evenings, when groups
item.content:encoded:
Residents living along Ratu Sukuna Road in Suva are raising concerns about speeding and reckless driving, particularly during weekends when the seawall area becomes a popular recreational area.

Ratu Sukuna Road resident Marita Manley, who regularly walks and runs along the seawall with her dog, says the problem is particularly noticeable on Saturday and Sunday afternoons and evenings, when groups of young men gather along the road.

Manley says some drivers appear to use the area to race or speed their vehicles despite it being a residential road used by families and people visiting the seawall.

She says the situation is concerning for families with young children, many of whom ride bicycles and scooters along the seawall.

Recently, some accidents have also occurred in the Nasese area.

Manley says the seawall is one of the few recreational spaces available in Suva where people can walk, exercise and have picnics, and she believes the behaviour of a small group of drivers is affecting the enjoyment of the area for others.

She says the Fiji Roads Authority had to install traffic-calming measures after the road was upgraded because of the way some drivers were using the road.

Manley says it is unfortunate that these measures affect everyone because of the behaviour of a relatively small group of drivers.

She says she has seen LTA traffic officers conduct operations in the area on Saturdays and Sundays at times , but believes a more consistent presence would be more effective.

Manley says the group of drivers involved is roughly the same and believes regular enforcement could help deter the behaviour.

She says drivers who want to drive like rally cars should use appropriate venues rather than public roads.

Manley says many families use the seawall, and she would be concerned if she were a parent of young children using the area.

She believes the behaviour could discourage families from enjoying the seawall, which is a public recreational space.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe says the Central Traffic Team has been conducting operations in the area, during which vehicles have been impounded and traffic infringement notices issued.

He says a team has been deployed to the area for the past two weeks.

Questions have been sent to Fiji Roads Authority and the Land Transport Authority.

item.title: Interim taxi fare adjustment to end on September 30th – FCCC
item.description: The interim taxi fare adjustment introduced in July this year will end on September 30th, with taxi operators required to return to the authorised fares from October 1st. The Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission says the temporary fare adjustment was introduced on July 1st in response to the significant increase in international fuel prices earlier this year.
item.content:encoded:
The interim taxi fare adjustment introduced in July this year will end on September 30th, with taxi operators required to return to the authorised fares from October 1st.

The Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission says the temporary fare adjustment was introduced on July 1st in response to the significant increase in international fuel prices earlier this year.

FCCC says the adjustment was approved to help taxi operators recover increased fuel costs while supporting the continued provision of reliable taxi services.

They say the measure was always intended to provide temporary relief while global fuel prices and their impact on Fiji’s taxi industry were monitored.

FCCC says taxi fares cannot be adjusted every time fuel prices change because any adjustment requires taxi meters around the country to be reprogrammed, tested and calibrated.

FCCC CEO Senikavika Jiuta says taxis play a vital role in Fiji’s transport network, particularly for people travelling to work, school, medical appointments, airports and areas with limited public transport.

She says FCCC has to strike a fair balance between protecting consumers from unjustified fare increases and ensuring taxi operators can continue providing safe, reliable and sustainable services.

FCCC says future major fare changes will undergo a full cost review, which will consider fuel costs as well as other factors affecting taxi operators.

They further say that any future fare adjustments will be assessed under FCCC’s established methodology and communicated publicly before being implemented.

FCCC is reminding taxi operators that from October 1st, only authorised taxi fares can be charged and meters must be recalibrated before then to avoid passengers being overcharged.

People who believe they have been overcharged can contact FCCC on 8921991 or or via email at helpdesk@fccc.gov.fj.

item.title: Live tsunami siren test for Suva–Lami corridor today, no evacuation required
item.description: The National Disaster Risk Management Office will be conducting live tsunami tests for the Suva–Lami corridor today between 10am and 12pm. A total of 13 tsunami sirens installed along the Suva foreshore will be activated during the test.
item.content:encoded:
The National Disaster Risk Management Office will be conducting live tsunami tests for the Suva–Lami corridor today between 10am and 12pm.

A total of 13 tsunami sirens installed along the Suva foreshore will be activated during the test.

The siren locations include key public and institutional sites such as the Water Authority of Fiji - Kinoya Sewerage Plant, FINTEL in Vatuwaqa, RFMF Officers Training School in Vatuwaqa, USP Lower Campus, USP Statham Campus, USP main campus, Veiuto Primary School, Government Training Centre in Nasese, i-Taukei Trust Fund Board, SCC Civic Carpark rooftop, Biosecurity in Suva Central, Government Shpping Services in Walu Bay and Lami Town.

People should be calm as no evacuation is required .

item.title: Dialogue Fiji launches two constitutional literacy publications to help Fijians make informed decisions
item.description: Many Fijians being asked to make submissions to the Constitution Review Commission do not even understand what a constitution is, what it is supposed to contain or how it affects their lives, raising concerns about how people can meaningfully participate in deciding Fiji’s constitutional future. Dialogue Fiji Executive Director Nilesh Lal says this is not the fault of ordinary Fijians but the resu
item.content:encoded:
Many Fijians being asked to make submissions to the Constitution Review Commission do not even understand what a constitution is, what it is supposed to contain or how it affects their lives, raising concerns about how people can meaningfully participate in deciding Fiji’s constitutional future.

Dialogue Fiji Executive Director Nilesh Lal says this is not the fault of ordinary Fijians but the result of the country not investing enough in constitutional literacy and civic education.

Lal highlighted this during the launch of two constitutional literacy publications by Dialogue Fiji at Tanoa Plaza in Suva.

He says constitutions have largely remained documents for lawyers, politicians and academics and are often written in complicated legal language that is not clearly explained to ordinary citizens.

Lal says people cannot simply be asked what kind of constitution they want without first being given the information they need to make an informed assessment.

He says another concern is that many people have strong views about whether a particular constitution is good or bad, but when asked which provisions they support or oppose, they often do not know.

Lal says in many cases, people have never read the constitution they feel strongly about, and their views are instead shaped by the politicians they support.

He says people should examine what a constitution actually provides, including how it distributes power, protects rights, establishes Parliament, controls the Executive, provides for the appointment of independent institutions and can be amended.

Lal says a constitution should not be treated like a political party manifesto, a tribal badge or a test of loyalty to one political camp because it belongs to the entire country.

He says constitutional discussions should be based on what the actual texts provide rather than political slogans, misinformation and blind loyalty to political leaders.

Dialogue Fiji has launched Fiji’s Recent Constitutional Frameworks: Comparing the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft, and the 2013 Constitution , which places the major provisions of the three frameworks side by side.

The publication compares areas including the Bills of Rights, electoral systems, Parliament, the Executive, the Judiciary, state services, accountability institutions, constitutional amendment procedures and the role of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga.

A second publication, Understanding Fiji’s Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide , uses illustrations, comparative tables and plain language to make constitutional issues easier for ordinary Fijians to understand.

Lal says the publications do not tell people which constitution they should support but allow them to examine individual provisions and decide for themselves what they believe is best suited for Fiji.

Lal says for Fiji, constitutional literacy is not simply an academic exercise but is essential to the protection and survival of democracy.

While launching the books, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says an informed citizenry is better equipped to participate constructively in national discussions and to exercise democratic rights responsibly.

Kamikamica says one of the greatest strengths of the publications is that they do not tell readers which constitution is best or advocate for the retention, amendment or replacement of any constitution, but instead provide information and leave the evaluation to readers.

He says Fiji's history shows that the legitimacy of a constitution and public trust in it are inseparable from the openness of the process through which it is produced or reviewed.

Kamikamica says constitutional discussions should be informed by facts, conducted respectfully and guided by a shared commitment to the national interest.

He says as Fiji moves forward, the Government is guided by the principle that the constitutional process must belong to the people of Fiji and not to any one office, political party or individual.

Kamikamica also encouraged young Fijians to read and understand the publications, saying the future of Fiji's democracy belongs to the next generation.

Associate Professor Dr Sandra Tarte from the University of the South Pacific's School of Law and Social Sciences says Fiji's constitutional journey has been long and, at times, difficult.

Tarte says in Fiji's relatively short history as an independent state, there have been fewer than three elected governments per constitution, and none of the country's constitutions has yet withstood the test of time, political turmoil, elections and authoritarian rule.

She highlighted how Fiji's constitutional arrangements have changed over the years, including the move from ethnically based electoral rolls under earlier constitutions to the common roll contained in the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution.

Tarte also highlighted the changing role of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga or Great Council of Chiefs, from having certain legislative and executive powers under the 1997 Constitution to a proposed advisory role under the Ghai Draft and being absent from the 2013 Constitution.

item.title: FEO warns AI election predictions could influence voters as specialist develops 12-factor forecasting model
item.description: AI-generated election predictions could influence undecided voters, affect voter turnout and create a misleading impression of certainty, according to the Fijian Elections Office, as a data analytics specialist demonstrates how AI and machine learning could be used to forecast Fiji’s next General Election. Fijian Elections Office Manager Legal Mesake Dawai says artificial intelligence is already p
item.content:encoded:
AI-generated election predictions could influence undecided voters, affect voter turnout and create a misleading impression of certainty, according to the Fijian Elections Office, as a data analytics specialist demonstrates how AI and machine learning could be used to forecast Fiji’s next General Election.

Fijian Elections Office Manager Legal Mesake Dawai says artificial intelligence is already present in Fiji’s election environment, with political parties using AI-generated images and other tools to develop campaign messages.

This comes as Data Analytics Specialist David Elbourne has developed a 12-factor prediction model which uses political trends, previous election results, social media sentiment, leader credibility, party resources and voter patterns to assess possible election outcomes.

Speaking during a presentation at the University of Fiji Press Club , which is led by students studying Journalism and Media at the University , Elbourne says the model looks at factors including political leaders’ credibility, online visibility, controversies, funding and resources, the spread of candidates around the country, iTaukei support and previous election performance.

He stresses that the model is not an opinion poll and does not provide a 100 percent certain election result.

Elbourne says it instead combines qualitative and quantitative data to identify trends and calculate probabilities based on available information.

He says there are several factors that cannot be accurately predicted, including final voter turnout, voters switching their support, the election date, political party alliances, future events, the impact of campaigns and how individuals eventually vote.

Elbourne says the model does not remove uncertainty but measures it, allowing analysts to assess what is known against factors that remain unknown.

However, Dawai says from the perspective of the Elections Office, the use of technology to predict election outcomes raise concerns about its potential impact on voters and the electoral process.

He says the Electoral Commission activated the campaign period on 25th May, and political parties are now allowed to campaign.

Dawai says while AI provides opportunities for innovation and is already being used by political parties, it needs to be used responsibly.

Insert: Dawai on Party using AI 10 Aug 26

He says the Elections Office would be concerned if AI or other predictive tools were used to publish claims about who would win the 2026 or 2027 national elections.

Dawai says Section 110 of the Electoral Act makes it unlawful for anyone to publish the results of election-related opinion polls during the seven days before polling day and on polling day until polling has closed at all polling stations.

He says this type of blackout period is not unique to Fiji, with similar restrictions used in other countries.

Dawai says election predictions and opinion polls could influence undecided voters who have registered but have not yet decided who they will vote for.

He says they could also affect voter turnout as some people may decide there is no point in voting if they believe a particular party is already going to win.

Dawai says another concern is that predictions could create a misleading impression of certainty, while statistical estimates can also be affected or manipulated.

He says the restriction is about protecting voters and the integrity of the final stage of the election.

Dawai stresses that the Elections Office is not against artificial intelligence, but its use during the electoral process must be responsible.

He says democracy is about people making their own choices regardless of how accurately others believe they can predict the result, adding the accuracy of any prediction can only be determined once the election outcome is known.

Meanwhile, Elbourne says the predictive framework could be updated regularly as new information becomes available and could be used by political parties, journalists, analysts, policymakers and academic institutions to monitor changing trends.

He says similar predictive models could also be applied outside elections in areas such as climate change, economic development, infrastructure projects and government policy.

Elbourne also highlighted the wider impact of artificial intelligence, saying around 60 percent of jobs are directly impacted by AI.

He says universities need to move beyond the traditional approach of students enrolling, attending lectures, graduating and entering the workforce.

Elbourne is calling for Fiji to develop what he describes as "high-value universities", where institutions use research, data, artificial intelligence and local talent to tackle complex problems facing the country and develop practical solutions.

He says universities should create their own intellectual property from these ideas and frameworks, while students and academic institutions should be willing to ask difficult questions about Fiji’s economy, governance, policies and politics.

Elbourne says Fiji has the talent and capability to participate in the AI revolution but needs the innovation, courage and drive to take advantage of the opportunities it presents.

He is encouraging universities, students, policymakers and other institutions to develop locally created frameworks and intellectual property that can help address Fiji’s challenges.
